input:
Raoult's law provides a simple and convenient method for estimating the partial pressure of a component in an ideal liquid mixture, and it is applied here to a mixture of hexane in heptane. The law is expressed by the equation

$$p = x P^*$$

where $p$ is the partial pressure of the volatile component, $x$ is its mole fraction in the liquid, and $P^*$ is the vapour pressure of the pure component at the temperature of the mixture. In this case, the liquid mole fraction of the volatile component is $x$ = 0.43, and the pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature is $P^*$ = 20.1 kPa. Multiplying the mole fraction of 0.43 by the pure-component vapour pressure of 20.1 kPa gives the partial pressure as $p$ = 8.6 kPa. The law is attractive in practice because it reduces the whole problem to two quantities that are either known from the composition of the mixture or readily available from standard tables of physical properties, and it is very widely used as a first estimate in vapour-liquid equilibrium calculations of all kinds. It is important to note that Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules are the same as those between like molecules. For a real mixture, this assumption is not generally exact, and activity coefficients would be used to correct the result; in the present calculation, however, no activity coefficients have been applied, so the value of 8.6 kPa should be understood as the ideal-solution estimate for the mixture at $x$ = 0.43 only.
target:
An ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane holds the volatile component at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.43. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure $p$ as

$$p = x P^*$$

where $p$ is the partial pressure, $x$ is the liquid mole fraction of the volatile component and $P^*$ is its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. Substitution gives $p$ = 0.43 × 20.1 kPa = 8.6 kPa. Raoult's law holds for an ideal solution. The partial pressure is the share of the total pressure over the mixture that the volatile component accounts for, and it is the quantity that links the liquid composition to the composition of the vapour in equilibrium with the liquid: a higher partial pressure for hexane means a vapour richer in hexane, at the same total pressure. Heptane enters the calculation only through the mole fraction. Its own vapour pressure does not appear in the stated data, because the partial pressure of the volatile component is fixed by its own mole fraction and its own pure-component vapour pressure alone. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied in this calculation, so 8.6 kPa is the ideal-solution value: the partial pressure of the real mixture departs from it by the activity coefficient of the volatile component, which multiplies the ideal value and which the stated data do not supply. A mixture in which unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than like molecules holds the volatile component back and gives a lower partial pressure; a mixture with weaker unlike attraction gives a higher one. The result is used as the ideal reference against which a corrected value would be compared, and not as the partial pressure of the actual hexane and heptane mixture at $x$ = 0.43 and the stated temperature.
